subject: rla
title: The Extended Response II: Organizing, Revising, and Full RLA Review
objectives: Students will organize an extended response into an introduction with a thesis, body paragraphs, and a conclusion.
Students will support each body paragraph with specific, accurately quoted or paraphrased evidence from both passages and explain why the evidence is strong or weak.
Students will follow a timed-writing plan that fits reading, planning, drafting, and revising into 45 minutes.
Students will revise for ideas and organization and then edit for grammar, usage, and mechanics in the final minutes.
Students will review the full range of RLA reading, argument analysis, and language skills in preparation for test day.
teach:
Lesson overview

Week 10 is the final week of the course. In Week 9, learners practiced reading two opposing arguments, deciding which one is better supported, and writing a thesis that states that judgment. This week they turn that plan into a complete, organized response inside the 45-minute limit: an introduction, body paragraphs built on specific evidence, a conclusion, and a short but disciplined revision and editing pass. Because the essay draws on nearly every RLA skill in the course (main idea, evidence, author's purpose, tone, argument analysis, comparing texts, and grammar), it is also the natural place for a cumulative review. Tell learners at the start: “The essay is where everything you have learned this course comes together.”

The lesson uses this week's paired passages on a new issue: whether the fictional city of Harlow should require employers with fifteen or more workers to post a pay range in every job ad. Passage A (Okafor) is the better-supported argument; Passage B (Whitlock) relies on an anecdote, unsupported predictions, a slippery slope, and a vague appeal to what “many business owners” think, though it does raise one fair point about the pilot's volunteers. Have learners read both passages before the lesson if possible.

Objectives

  • Organize an extended response into an introduction, two or three body paragraphs, and a conclusion.
  • Write body paragraphs that name, cite, and explain specific evidence from both passages.
  • Follow a timed-writing plan that fits reading, planning, drafting, and revising into 45 minutes.
  • Revise for ideas and organization, then edit for grammar and mechanics, in the last minutes.
  • Review the full range of RLA reading, argument, and grammar skills.

Materials

  • Student Lesson, this week's Notes sheet, and practice Passages A and B (printed or on screen)
  • A timer visible to the class
  • Highlighters in two colors (one for claims, one for evidence)
  • Copies of the guided-practice paragraph (below)
  • The Week 10 practice items; items 1–6 are used for independent practice

Note: A full 45-minute timed response does not fit inside a 60-minute lesson. Today you teach the plan and practice its parts; learners complete a full timed response at home (Day 2 of the study plan) and bring it to the next meeting for feedback.

Warm-up (5 minutes): Where does it go?

Display these four sentences. Learners label each one Introduction, Body, Conclusion, or Delete.

  1. Okafor reports that 37 of the 40 pilot employers planned to keep posting ranges after the program ended.
  2. The two writers disagree about whether Harlow should require pay ranges in job ads.
  3. I once applied for a job that paid way less than I expected, so I agree with Okafor.
  4. Taken together, Okafor's data and her answer to critics make hers the stronger argument.

Answers: 1 Body (specific evidence). 2 Introduction (frames the issue). 3 Delete (personal opinion and experience; the task is to judge the arguments, not the issue). 4 Conclusion (sums up the judgment). Spend the most time on sentence 3: it is the mistake that costs the most points on Trait 1.

Direct instruction (20 minutes)

Talking point 1: The 45-minute plan (4 minutes)

Say: “The biggest reason good readers score low on the essay is that they run out of time. A plan protects you.” Write the plan on the board:

MinutesTask
0–8Read the prompt, then both passages. Mark each writer's claim, best evidence, and weak spots.
8–13Decide which argument is better supported. Write the thesis. List two or three body-paragraph points with the evidence for each.
13–38Draft: introduction (about 3 minutes), body paragraphs (about 6–7 minutes each), conclusion (about 3 minutes).
38–45Revise (about 3 minutes), then edit (about 4 minutes).

Stress that the plan is a guide, not a cage. If reading takes ten minutes, cut a minute from each body paragraph, never from the conclusion or the edit.

Talking point 2: The response blueprint (4 minutes)

  • Introduction (2–4 sentences): frame the issue, name both writers and their positions, and end with the thesis.
  • Body 1: the better-supported writer's strongest evidence, and why it is strong.
  • Body 2: the other writer's evidence, and why it is weaker (anecdote, prediction, vague source, faulty reasoning).
  • Body 3 (optional, if time allows): admit the weaker side's best point and explain why it does not change your judgment.
  • Conclusion (2–3 sentences): restate the judgment in new words and sum up the reasons. No new evidence.

Talking point 3: PEEL body paragraphs (4 minutes)

Every body paragraph follows the same pattern. Point: a topic sentence that makes one claim about the quality of support. Evidence: a short quotation or a precise paraphrase, with attribution (“Okafor reports …”). Explain: one or two sentences on why this evidence is strong or weak. Link: tie it back to the thesis. Remind learners that the “Explain” step is where most of the score lives; quoting without explaining is just copying.

Talking point 4: Specific evidence (4 minutes)

Contrast on the board: Vague: “Okafor has a lot of facts.” Specific: “Okafor reports that the average time to fill a job fell from 41 days to 33 days during a six-month pilot with 40 employers.” Specific evidence names the source, uses the passage's own numbers or words, and is accurate. Teach three attribution verbs to vary the writing: reports, argues, claims. Note that “claims” is useful for weak evidence (“Whitlock claims that many owners agree”).

Talking point 5: The last seven minutes (4 minutes)

Revise before you edit. Revise (big things, about 3 minutes): Is the thesis clear? Does each body paragraph's first sentence support it? Is there any sentence about my own opinion on the issue? Delete it. Edit (small things, about 4 minutes): read each sentence once, looking for fragments, run-ons and comma splices, subject-verb agreement, confused words (their/there/they're, its/it's, then/than, a lot), and capitalization of names. Tell learners that the response box does not check spelling, so their own eyes are the only spell checker.

Worked examples

Example 1: Building the plan in five minutes

Model a T-chart for Passages A and B, thinking aloud.

Okafor (A): for the ordinanceWhitlock (B): against
Pilot, 40 employers: 22% fewer applicants who refused the pay; 41 to 33 days to fillOne story: the press operator
County review: men/women starting-pay gap about half as largePrediction: workers “will demand raises” (no evidence)
Answers critics: under-15 exemption; range not exact salary; 37 of 40 kept postingSlippery slope: city will tell us “what to pay”; vague “many business owners I know”
Fair point: pilot employers volunteered

Thesis: Okafor's argument is better supported because she relies on measured results and answers her critics, while Whitlock relies on one story and predictions he never supports.

Outline: Body 1, Okafor's pilot data and county review. Body 2, Whitlock's anecdote, prediction, and slippery slope. Body 3, Whitlock's volunteer point and why it does not outweigh Okafor's evidence. Total planning time: about five minutes.

Example 2: Making evidence specific

Before: “Okafor shows that pay ranges are fair. She has good evidence about this and it proves her point.”

Think aloud: Which evidence? From where? Why is it good? Find paragraph 3 of Passage A and use its exact facts.

After: “Okafor also argues that pay ranges make hiring fairer. She cites a review of hiring records by the Marsh County Labor Office, which found that the gap between men's and women's starting pay was about half as large at employers that posted ranges. Because this finding comes from actual hiring records rather than opinions, it gives readers solid reason to accept her claim.”

What changed: a clear point; a named source; the passage's own finding; an explanation of why the evidence is strong.

Example 3: A seven-minute revision and edit

Draft conclusion: “In conclusion Okafor is right and Whitlock is wrong. Pay ranges is a good idea and the city council should pass it. Their is no reason not too.”

Revise first (big): The conclusion judges the issue (“is right,” “good idea”) instead of the support. Rewrite it to restate the thesis and reasons.

Then edit (small): add a comma after “In conclusion”; “Pay ranges is” has a subject-verb error; “city council” should be “City Council” when naming Harlow's council; “Their” should be “There”; “too” should be “to.”

Revised: “In conclusion, Okafor's argument is the better supported of the two. She backs her claims with results from a real pilot and a review of hiring records, while Whitlock depends on one story and predictions he never supports.”

Guided practice (15 minutes)

Display this body paragraph. As a group, first revise (ideas and organization), then edit (grammar and mechanics).

“Whitlock's argument is not as good. He talks about a worker he hired and he thinks the range will lock people in. He also says employees will want raises which is a problem for there business. Its just a prediction. Alot of business owners agree with him though.”

Answers. Revise: (1) The topic sentence is vague; replace it with a claim about support: “Whitlock's argument rests on much weaker support than Okafor's.” (2) “Talks about a worker” should name and explain the evidence: one press operator, one shop, so it cannot show what will happen citywide. (3) “Alot of business owners agree with him” repeats Whitlock's vague claim as if it were fact; instead, evaluate it: he never says who these owners are or how many. (4) Add a linking sentence back to the thesis. Edit: the compound sentence “He talks about a worker he hired and he thinks …” needs a comma before “and”; “raises which” needs a comma (“raises, which”); “there” should be “their”; “Its” should be “It's” (or, better, “This is”); “Alot” should be “A lot.”

Model revision: “Whitlock's argument rests on much weaker support. To show that a posted range ‘locks both sides in,’ he describes hiring a single press operator, but one hire at one shop cannot show what will happen across a city. He also predicts that employees ‘will demand raises,’ yet he gives no numbers or examples. Finally, he says that ‘many business owners I know agree,’ but he never says who they are or how many. Each of these weaknesses leaves his claims unproven, which is why Okafor's evidence is more convincing.”

Independent practice (15 minutes)

Learners complete practice items 1–6. Circulate. On item 6, ask anyone who chose the “workers deserve to know” thesis: “Does that sentence judge the evidence or the issue?” Items 7–12 (editing the draft response, organization, conclusions, and counterarguments) are assigned for Day 4 of the study plan.

Checks for understanding

  • Q: What are the four parts of the 45-minute plan? Expected: read and mark (about 8 min), plan and thesis (about 5), draft (about 25), revise and edit (about 7).
  • Q: What does PEEL stand for, and which part do writers most often skip? Expected: Point, Evidence, Explain, Link; they skip Explain.
  • Q: Why should you revise before you edit? Expected: fixing commas in a sentence you later delete wastes time; big problems cost more points.
  • Q: Can your response argue that the weaker-supported side is right about the issue? Expected: The task is to judge which argument is better supported. You may personally agree with either side, but the response must be about the quality of the support.
  • Q: What should a conclusion never do? Expected: add new evidence, switch positions, or tell readers to decide for themselves.

Common mistakes and how to correct them

  • Arguing the issue instead of the evidence. Learners write “Pay ranges are good because …” Correct by asking, “Whose evidence is stronger, and why?” Ban the words “I think” and “I believe” on the essay.
  • Quoting without explaining. A paragraph of quotations scores like a summary. Correct with the PEEL rule: every piece of evidence gets at least one “because” or “this shows” sentence.
  • Ignoring the weaker side. The prompt says to analyze both positions. Correct by requiring at least one paragraph on the weaker writer's evidence.
  • Never finishing. A missing conclusion hurts Trait 2. Correct with the timer: at minute 35, start the conclusion no matter what.
  • Skipping the edit. Learners stop writing at 44:59. Correct by practicing the 38-minute alarm until it is a habit.
  • Misquoting. Learners quote from memory and change numbers. Correct by teaching them to copy short phrases exactly and check numbers against the passage.

Differentiation

Support: Give learners sentence frames: “[Writer] argues that … ” / “To support this claim, [writer] reports that … ” / “This evidence is strong (or weak) because … ” / “Therefore, [writer]'s argument is better supported.” Allow a 55-minute first timed response, then cut five minutes each attempt. Stretch: Require a third body paragraph that concedes the weaker writer's best point (Whitlock's volunteer criticism) and answers it. Ask advanced learners to vary sentence openings and use at least three transition types (addition, contrast, cause).

How this shows up on the GED

The RLA test includes one Extended Response with its own time limit of about 45 minutes. The prompt gives two passages that take opposite positions and asks learners to “analyze both positions … to determine which one is best supported,” using “relevant and specific evidence from both articles.” The response is scored on three traits: Trait 1, creation of arguments and use of evidence; Trait 2, development and organizational structure; and Trait 3, clarity and command of standard English. Each trait is worth up to 2 points. This week's lesson maps directly onto the traits: specific evidence and explanation (Trait 1), the blueprint and transitions (Trait 2), and the editing pass (Trait 3). The same editing skills appear in the multiple-choice and drop-down language items elsewhere on the test, so every minute spent on editing practice pays off twice. The response is typed in a box with basic tools such as cut, copy, paste, undo, and redo, but no spell check.
student:
Where you are now

Last week you learned to read two opposing arguments, decide which one is better supported, and write a thesis that states your judgment. This week you will turn that plan into a complete response in 45 minutes: an organized essay with specific evidence, plus a quick revision and edit at the end. Before you start, read Passage A and Passage B in this week's practice. They are about whether the city of Harlow should require larger employers to list a pay range in every job ad. All of the examples below use them.

Your 45-minute plan

MinutesWhat to do
0–8Read. Read the prompt first, then both passages. Mark each writer's claim, best evidence, and weak spots.
8–13Plan. Decide which argument is better supported. Write your thesis. List two or three body-paragraph points and the evidence for each.
13–38Draft. Introduction (about 3 min), body paragraphs (about 6–7 min each), conclusion (about 3 min).
38–45Revise, then edit. About 3 minutes on big problems, about 4 on small ones.

Strategy: If you fall behind, shorten a body paragraph. Never skip the conclusion or the final edit. A complete response with a short conclusion scores better than an unfinished one.

The blueprint of a strong response

  • Introduction: frame the issue, name both writers and their positions, end with your thesis.
  • Body paragraph 1: the stronger writer's best evidence and why it is strong.
  • Body paragraph 2: the weaker writer's evidence and why it is weak.
  • Body paragraph 3 (if time allows): admit the weaker writer's best point, then explain why it does not change your judgment.
  • Conclusion: restate your judgment in new words and sum up your reasons. No new evidence.

Remember: The task is to judge which argument is better supported, not which side you agree with. Leave out “I think,” “I believe,” and stories from your own life.

Building body paragraphs: PEEL

  1. Point: one claim about the quality of a writer's support.
  2. Evidence: a short, exact quotation or a precise paraphrase, with the writer's name (“Okafor reports …”).
  3. Explain: why this evidence is strong or weak. This is the most important step.
  4. Link: connect back to your thesis.

Vague evidence vs. specific evidence

Vague (weak)Specific (strong)
Okafor has a lot of facts.Okafor reports that the average time to fill a job fell from 41 days to 33 days during the pilot.
Whitlock just tells a story.Whitlock supports his claim with the story of one press operator he hired last spring.
Whitlock says bad things will happen.Whitlock predicts that employees “will demand raises,” but he gives no numbers or examples.

Worked example 1: A five-minute plan

Okafor (A): pilot with 40 employers (22% fewer applicants who refused the pay; 41 to 33 days to fill); county review (men/women starting-pay gap about half as large); answers critics (under-15 exemption, range not exact salary).

Whitlock (B): one story (press operator); unsupported prediction (raises); slippery slope (city will set pay); vague “many business owners I know”; one fair point (pilot employers volunteered).

Thesis: Okafor's argument is better supported because she relies on measured results and answers her critics, while Whitlock relies on one story and unsupported predictions.

Worked example 2: A model response

Should employers have to tell job seekers what a job pays before they apply? In Harlow, the City Council is considering an ordinance that would require employers with fifteen or more workers to post a pay range in every job ad. Denise Okafor, director of the Harlow Workforce Center, supports the ordinance, while business owner Gary Whitlock opposes it. Okafor's argument is better supported because she backs her claims with results from a real pilot program and a review of hiring records, and she directly answers her opponents' main concern. Whitlock, by contrast, relies on a single personal story and predictions he never supports.

Okafor's strongest evidence comes from the Workforce Center's six-month pilot program with 40 employers. She reports that those employers received “22 percent fewer applications from people who later turned down an offer because the pay was too low” and that the average time to fill a job fell “from 41 days to 33 days.” These are measured results, not guesses, and they directly support her claim that posting pay saves time for both employers and applicants. She adds a review by the Marsh County Labor Office showing that the gap between men's and women's starting pay was about half as large at employers that posted ranges. Because this evidence comes from records rather than opinions, it gives readers a solid reason to accept her claim that pay ranges make hiring fairer.

Whitlock's argument, on the other hand, rests on much weaker support. To show that a posted range “locks both sides in,” he tells the story of one press operator he hired. One hire at one shop cannot show what will happen across an entire city, and his claim that she “might have” skipped the job is only a guess. He also predicts that employees “will demand raises” and that the city will soon start “telling us what to pay,” but he offers no numbers or examples. This is a slippery slope: it assumes one step will lead to a worse one without showing why. Finally, his statement that “many business owners I know agree” is vague, since readers never learn who these owners are or how many there are.

To be fair, Whitlock raises one reasonable point. The pilot employers volunteered, so their results might not match those of businesses that are required to post pay. However, he offers no evidence that the results would be different, and Okafor shows that the ordinance was written with small businesses in mind by exempting those with fewer than fifteen workers and requiring only a range.

In the end, Okafor's position is the better supported of the two. She uses measured results, credible records, and a direct answer to her critics, while Whitlock depends on one story, unsupported predictions, and vague claims of agreement. A reader looking for evidence, not just strong feelings, will find it in Okafor's article.

Why it works: The thesis judges the support, not the issue. Each body paragraph starts with a clear point. Every quotation is short, exact, and explained. The fourth paragraph admits Whitlock's best point and answers it. The conclusion restates the judgment without adding anything new.

Worked example 3: An annotated revision

First draft (written at minute 30):

“Whitlock's argument is not as good. He talks about a worker he hired and he thinks the range will lock people in. He also says employees will want raises which is a problem for there business. Its just a prediction. Alot of business owners agree with him though.”

Revision notes:

  1. Vague point. “Not as good” does not say why. Change to a claim about support.
  2. Vague evidence. “Talks about a worker” should name the evidence: one press operator.
  3. Missing explanation. Add why one story is weak evidence.
  4. Accepting a weak claim as fact. “Alot of business owners agree with him” repeats Whitlock's vague claim. Evaluate it instead.
  5. Editing errors. Comma before “and” in a compound sentence; comma before “which”; there to their; Its to It's; Alot to a lot.

Revised: “Whitlock's argument rests on much weaker support. To show that a posted range ‘locks both sides in,’ he describes hiring one press operator, but one hire at one shop cannot show what will happen across a city. He also predicts that employees ‘will demand raises,’ yet he gives no numbers or examples. His claim that ‘many business owners I know agree’ is vague, because he never says who they are or how many.”

The last seven minutes

Revise (big things, about 3 minutes)

  • Is my thesis clear, and does it judge the support?
  • Does each body paragraph begin with a point that backs the thesis?
  • Did I explain every piece of evidence?
  • Is there any sentence about my personal opinion? Delete it.

Edit (small things, about 4 minutes)

  • Fragments, run-ons, and comma splices
  • Subject-verb agreement (“the numbers support”)
  • Confused words: their/there/they're, its/it's, then/than, to/too, a lot
  • Capital letters for names and titles (Harlow City Council)
  • Exact quotations and numbers

Common mistake: Fixing commas first. If you later delete that sentence, the time is wasted. Revise, then edit.

Try it

1. It is minute 32. You have written your introduction and one body paragraph. What should you do?

Show answer

Write a short second body paragraph about the weaker writer's evidence (about 5 minutes), then a two- or three-sentence conclusion by about minute 38. Use the remaining minutes to revise and edit. Skip the optional third body paragraph.

2. Rewrite this vague sentence with specific evidence from Passage A: “Okafor shows that a lot of employers liked the pilot.”

Show answer

Sample: “Okafor reports that when the pilot ended, 37 of the 40 participating employers planned to keep posting pay ranges on their own.”

3. Edit this sentence. It has three errors: “Whitlock say that the pilot employers volunteered, this means there results might not apply to everyone.”

Show answer

“Whitlock says that the pilot employers volunteered, which means their results might not apply to everyone.” (Subject-verb agreement; the comma splice fixed with “which”; there changed to their.) Using a period or semicolon before “This means” also fixes the splice.

4. Why is this a weak thesis? “I agree with Okafor because I hate long job searches.”

Show answer

It gives a personal opinion and experience instead of judging which argument is better supported, and it names no evidence from either passage.

5. Review: Whitlock writes, “Many business owners I know agree that this rule could tear their teams apart.” Why is this weak evidence?

Show answer

It is vague. He does not say who the owners are, how many there are, or how he knows what they think, so readers cannot check it. It also appeals to popular opinion rather than facts.
post:
Summary of key points

  • Follow a 45-minute plan: read and mark (about 8 min), plan and thesis (about 5), draft (about 25), revise and edit (about 7).
  • Use the blueprint: introduction with thesis, body paragraphs on each writer's evidence, an optional paragraph that answers the weaker side's best point, and a short conclusion.
  • Build body paragraphs with PEEL: Point, Evidence, Explain, Link. The explanation earns the points.
  • Use specific evidence: the writer's name, exact words or numbers, and accurate paraphrase.
  • In the last minutes, revise before you edit.
  • Judge the support, not the issue. Leave your own opinion out.

Exit ticket

1. What goes in the last sentence of a typical introduction?

Show answer

The thesis: which argument is better supported, and a brief preview of why.

2. Name the four steps of a PEEL paragraph.

Show answer

Point, Evidence, Explain, Link.

3. Your essay timer reads 38 minutes. What should you be doing?

Show answer

Finishing the conclusion and starting to revise (big problems), then edit (small errors).

4. Correct this sentence: “Okafor's numbers comes from a real pilot, its not a guess.”

Show answer

“Okafor's numbers come from a real pilot; they are not a guess.” (Plural verb come; the comma splice fixed with a semicolon; its replaced, since “it's” would not agree with the plural “numbers.”)

5. Give one thing a conclusion should never do.

Show answer

Any one: add new evidence, switch positions, or tell readers to decide for themselves.

Reflection

  • Which part of the 45 minutes is hardest for you to finish on time? What will you change?
  • Look back at your Week 9 thesis practice. How has the way you write about evidence changed?
  • Which RLA skill from the whole course do you feel most confident about? Which one needs one more review?

Test-day strategy

  • Before: Sleep well, eat, bring the required identification, and arrive early so you start calm.
  • Pacing: Check the clock after each passage. If a question is taking too long, choose your best answer, flag it, and move on.
  • Answer everything: A blank answer earns nothing, so never leave a question empty.
  • Reading items: Read the question, form your own answer, then match it to a choice. Watch for answers that are too narrow, too broad, not stated, or distorted.
  • Editing items: Read the whole sentence with each option before choosing.
  • Extended Response: Follow your 45-minute plan. The essay has its own time limit, so unused minutes do not carry over; spend every remaining minute revising and editing.
  • Break: Stand up, drink water, and clear your head. Do not reread your essay in your mind.

Test-taking strategy: Set a 38-minute alarm in your head

When the essay clock shows about 7 minutes left, stop drafting, even mid-paragraph. Write one sentence to finish the thought, add a short conclusion if you do not have one, then revise and edit. Readers score what is on the page, and a finished, clean response almost always beats a longer one full of errors.

vocab.def: The essay part of the GED RLA test, in which you analyze two arguments and explain which is better supported, in about 45 minutes.
vocab.example: The Extended Response asks which article uses stronger evidence.

vocab.def: One sentence that states your judgment about which argument is better supported and briefly why.
vocab.example: Okafor's argument is better supported because she uses measured results.

vocab.def: The opening paragraph that frames the issue, names both writers and their positions, and ends with the thesis.
vocab.example: Two writers disagree about whether job ads should list pay.

vocab.def: A middle paragraph that makes one point and supports it with specific, explained evidence.
vocab.example: A paragraph showing why Whitlock's anecdote is weak evidence.

vocab.def: The first sentence of a body paragraph, which states the paragraph's main point.
vocab.example: Whitlock's argument rests on much weaker support.

vocab.def: The final paragraph that restates the judgment in new words and sums up the reasons without adding new evidence.
vocab.example: In the end, Okafor makes the stronger case.

vocab.def: Exact facts, numbers, or words from a passage, credited to the writer.
vocab.example: The time to fill a job fell from 41 days to 33 days.

vocab.def: Naming the source of a quotation or idea.
A writer's exact words, placed in quotation marks.
Restating a writer's idea accurately in your own words.
vocab.example: Okafor says most pilot employers planned to keep posting pay.

vocab.def: Admitting that the other side has a fair point, then explaining why it does not change your judgment.
vocab.example: To be fair, the pilot employers volunteered; however, …

vocab.def: Improving the ideas, evidence, and organization of a draft.
vocab.example: Replacing a vague topic sentence with a clear point.

vocab.def: Correcting grammar, usage, spelling, capitalization, and punctuation.
A schedule that divides the time limit among reading, planning, drafting, and revising.
vocab.example: Read 8 minutes, plan 5, draft 25, revise and edit 7.

notes:
Week 10 RLA Study Sheet: The Extended Response II and Full Review

45-minute plan

MinTask
0–8Read prompt and passages; mark claims, evidence, weak spots
8–13Choose better-supported side; thesis; outline
13–38Draft: intro, 2–3 body paragraphs, conclusion
38–45Revise (3 min), edit (4 min)

Blueprint

  1. Intro: issue, both writers, thesis
  2. Body: stronger writer's evidence
  3. Body: weaker writer's evidence
  4. Body (optional): answer the weaker side's best point
  5. Conclusion: restate judgment; no new evidence

PEEL body paragraph

Point → Evidence → Explain → Link

Strong vs. weak evidence

  • Strong: measured results, records, named sources, answers to the other side
  • Weak: one story, predictions with no support, “many people say,” emotional appeals
  • Faulty reasoning: slippery slope, hasty generalization, personal attack, bandwagon

Last-minute edit list

  • Fragments, run-ons, comma splices
  • Subject-verb and pronoun agreement
  • their/there/they're; its/it's; then/than; to/too; a lot
  • Capitalize names and titles
  • Exact quotes and numbers

Reading answer traps

Too narrow, too broad, not stated, distorted.

Scoring traits (0–2 each): Trait 1, arguments and evidence. Trait 2, development and organization. Trait 3, clarity and standard English.

Avoid: “I think”; arguing the issue instead of the support; quoting without explaining; skipping the weaker side; no conclusion; no edit.

Test day: pace by passage, answer every question, flag and return, and use every essay minute.

stimuli.title: Passage A: Post the Pay: Every Job Ad Should List a Salary Range
stimuli.html:
(1) Every week at the Harlow Workforce Center, I meet job seekers who have spent hours filling out applications, taking skills tests, and arranging child care for interviews, only to learn at the very end that the job pays far less than they can live on. That waste of time and effort is avoidable. The Harlow City Council should pass the proposed ordinance requiring every employer with fifteen or more workers to include a good-faith pay range in each job posting.

(2) Posted pay ranges save time for employers and applicants alike. Last year, the Workforce Center ran a six-month pilot program in which 40 local employers agreed to list pay ranges in their job ads. According to the center's final report, those employers received 22 percent fewer applications from people who later turned down an offer because the pay was too low. The average time it took them to fill an open position also fell, from 41 days to 33 days. Hiring managers told us they spent fewer hours interviewing candidates who were never going to accept.

(3) Pay ranges also make hiring fairer. When pay is kept secret, the workers who know the most about salaries, or who feel most comfortable negotiating, tend to get the best offers. Everyone else is left guessing. A review of hiring records by the Marsh County Labor Office found that among workers hired into the same job titles, the gap between men's and women's starting pay was about half as large at employers that posted ranges as at employers that did not.

(4) Some business owners worry that posting pay will expose private information or burden small shops. The ordinance was written with those concerns in mind. It does not apply to businesses with fewer than fifteen employees, and it requires a range, not an exact salary, so employers still have room to pay more for experience. In fact, when the pilot ended, 37 of the 40 participating employers said they planned to keep posting ranges on their own.

(5) Job seekers deserve to know what a job pays before they invest their time in applying. Employers deserve applicants who are ready to say yes. One line in every job ad serves both. The Council should pass the ordinance.
stimuli.source: By Denise Okafor, director of the Harlow Workforce Center (original passage written for KCE GED Prep)

stimuli.title: Passage B: Keep the City Out of Our Job Ads
stimuli.html:
(1) I have owned Whitlock Printing on Second Street for nineteen years. In that time I have hired dozens of people, and I have never once had trouble talking about pay with an applicant. Now the Harlow City Council wants to tell me how to write my own help-wanted ads. The proposed pay-range ordinance is a bad idea that will hurt the very businesses that keep this city working.

(2) Pay should be a conversation, not a number printed in advance. Every applicant brings different skills and experience to the table. Last spring, I hired a press operator who turned out to have ten years of experience I had not expected, so I paid her well above what I had planned. If I had posted a range, she might have looked at the top number, decided it was too low, and never applied at all. A posted range locks both sides in before they have even met.

(3) The ordinance will also cause trouble inside workplaces. When current employees see a posting with a range higher than what they earn, they will demand raises, and owners who cannot afford them will lose good people. Many business owners I know agree that this rule could tear their teams apart. And once the city controls our job ads, it will not be long before it starts telling us what to pay.

(4) Supporters like to point to the Workforce Center's pilot program. But the 40 employers in that program volunteered, which means they were already comfortable posting pay. Of course it worked for them. Their experience tells us nothing about what will happen when every business is forced to follow the rule, whether it wants to or not.

(5) Harlow's employers are not the enemy. We take the risks, we meet the payroll, and we create the jobs this city depends on. The Council should trust us to treat our workers fairly and vote no on this ordinance.
stimuli.source: By Gary Whitlock, owner of Whitlock Printing and member of the Harlow Small Business Alliance (original passage written for KCE GED Prep)

stimuli.title: Draft Response: Which Argument Is Better Supported?
stimuli.html:
A GED learner wrote this response to Passages A and B in 45 minutes. It has not yet been revised or edited. Blanks (A) through (E) mark places to be edited.

(1) Should employers in Harlow be required to list pay ranges in their job ads? Denise Okafor, director of the Harlow Workforce Center, argues that they should, while print shop owner Gary Whitlock argues that the city should stay out of hiring. Okafor's argument is better supported because she relies on measured results and answers her opponents' concerns, while Whitlock relies mostly on one personal story and predictions he does not back up.

(2) Okafor's evidence comes from a real test, not a guess. (A) the employers in her pilot program received 22 percent fewer applications from people who would reject the pay, they filled jobs faster, dropping from 41 days to 33 days. Personally, I think every job ad should list the pay, because I hate wasting time on applications. Okafor also cites a county review showing that the pay gap between men and women hired into the same jobs was about half as large at employers that posted ranges. These numbers (B) her claim that pay ranges make hiring both faster and fairer.

(3) Whitlock's argument is weaker. He describes hiring a press operator who had more experience than he expected, but one story about one hire cannot show what will happen across a whole city. He also predicts that the ordinance will lead the city to control (C) no evidence for this prediction. To be fair, Whitlock makes one strong point: the employers in the pilot volunteered, so (D) results may not apply to every business. Even so, one reasonable doubt does not outweigh Okafor's data, and Whitlock offers no numbers of his own.

(4) In conclusion, both writers care about Harlow's workers and businesses, but Okafor makes the stronger case. The (E) should look closely at the evidence each writer provides. That is my opinion about the two articles.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses Okafor's main claim in Passage A?
options: The Harlow City Council should require employers with fifteen or more workers to list a pay range in every job posting.
All employers in Harlow should be required to raise the pay they offer to new workers.
The Workforce Center's pilot program should be expanded to include every employer in Marsh County.
Job seekers should learn to negotiate their pay before they accept an offer.
items.hint: Look at the last sentence of paragraph 1 and the last sentence of paragraph 5. What does Okafor ask the Council to do?
items.explain:
Step 1. Find where Okafor states her position. The last sentence of paragraph 1 says the Council “should pass the proposed ordinance requiring every employer with fifteen or more workers to include a good-faith pay range in each job posting.” Paragraph 5 repeats: “The Council should pass the ordinance.”

Step 2. Match that claim to a choice: requiring employers with fifteen or more workers to list a pay range. Correct.

Step 3. Check the traps. Raising pay is distorted: the ordinance requires posting a range, not paying more. Expanding the pilot is not stated. Learning to negotiate is not stated; Okafor actually argues that secret pay hurts people who are uncomfortable negotiating.

items.prompt: In paragraph 2 of Passage B, Whitlock claims that “a posted range locks both sides in before they have even met.” Which type of evidence does he mainly use to support this claim?
options: A personal story about one employee he hired
Statistics from a survey of local business owners
Testimony from an expert in labor economics
Results from a program in which employers posted pay ranges
items.hint: Reread paragraph 2. Does Whitlock give any numbers, name any experts, or describe a study?
items.explain:
Step 1. List what paragraph 2 contains: a general claim that applicants bring different skills, then the story of the press operator he hired “last spring,” then a guess about what “might have” happened if he had posted a range.

Step 2. The only support is a single personal experience, an anecdote. Correct.

Step 3. Eliminate the rest. Whitlock gives no survey statistics and names no expert. A program in which employers posted ranges is Okafor's evidence (the pilot), not Whitlock's; he mentions it only in paragraph 4, to criticize it.

items.prompt: Click the sentence from paragraph 2 of Passage A that gives the most specific evidence that posting pay ranges helped employers fill jobs faster.
spans: Posted pay ranges save time for employers and applicants alike.
Last year, the Workforce Center ran a six-month pilot program in which 40 local employers agreed to list pay ranges in their job ads.
According to the center's final report, those employers received 22 percent fewer applications from people who later turned down an offer because the pay was too low.
The average time it took them to fill an open position also fell, from 41 days to 33 days.
Hiring managers told us they spent fewer hours interviewing candidates who were never going to accept.
items.hint: “Filling jobs faster” is about time. Which sentence measures time with numbers?
items.explain:
Step 1. The question asks about filling jobs faster, so the evidence must measure how long hiring took.

Step 2. Only one sentence gives a measured time: “The average time it took them to fill an open position also fell, from 41 days to 33 days.” Correct. That is a drop of 8 days.

Step 3. Check the others. Sentence 1 is the paragraph's claim, not evidence. Sentence 2 describes the pilot but gives no result. Sentence 3 gives a number, but it measures applications from people who turned down offers, not hiring speed. Sentence 5 is related, but “fewer hours” is general and unmeasured, so it is less specific than the 41-to-33-day figure.

items.prompt: Which sentence from Passage B is an example of a slippery slope, a claim that one step will inevitably lead to a more extreme result without evidence that it will?
options: “And once the city controls our job ads, it will not be long before it starts telling us what to pay.”
“Every applicant brings different skills and experience to the table.”
“But the 40 employers in that program volunteered, which means they were already comfortable posting pay.”
“I have owned Whitlock Printing on Second Street for nineteen years.”
items.hint: Look for a sentence that predicts a chain of events: if this happens, then something bigger will follow.
items.explain:
Step 1. A slippery slope says that step A will lead to a more extreme step B, without showing how or why.

Step 2. “Once the city controls our job ads, it will not be long before it starts telling us what to pay” moves from one step (requiring pay ranges in ads) to a much bigger one (the city setting wages). Whitlock gives no evidence that the second step is planned or likely. Correct.

Step 3. The other sentences are not predictions. “Every applicant brings different skills” is a reasonable general statement. The point about volunteers is a fair criticism of Okafor's evidence. The nineteen-years sentence gives Whitlock's background.

items.prompt: A learner's thesis states: “Okafor's argument is better supported than Whitlock's.” Select two details from the passages that would best support this thesis in a body paragraph.
options: Okafor reports that during the pilot, the average time to fill an open position fell from 41 days to 33 days.
Okafor answers the worry about small shops by explaining that the ordinance does not apply to businesses with fewer than fifteen employees and requires only a range.
Whitlock has owned his printing business for nineteen years and has hired dozens of people.
Whitlock points out that the employers in the pilot program volunteered to post pay ranges.
Okafor says that job seekers “deserve to know what a job pays.”
Whitlock says that employers “create the jobs this city depends on.”
items.hint: Choose details that show Okafor using evidence or answering the other side, not details that help Whitlock or only state a value.
items.explain:
Step 1. The thesis is about support, so the best details show Okafor backing her claims with evidence or answering objections.

Step 2. The 41-to-33-day result is measured evidence from a real program. Correct. Okafor's explanation of the fifteen-employee limit and the range requirement directly answers her opponents' concern. Correct.

Step 3. Eliminate the rest. Whitlock's nineteen years and his point about volunteers help his credibility or argument, so they work against this thesis. Okafor's “deserve to know” line and Whitlock's “create the jobs” line are statements of values, not evidence.

items.prompt: Which sentence would be the most effective thesis statement for a response to the prompt: “Analyze both positions presented in the articles to determine which one is best supported”?
options: Okafor's argument is better supported because she backs her claims with results from a real pilot program and answers her opponents' concerns, while Whitlock relies mainly on one personal story and unsupported predictions.
Employers should have to post pay ranges because workers deserve to know what a job pays.
Both writers make some good points about pay ranges, and each argument has strengths and weaknesses.
This essay will discuss two articles about whether job ads should include pay ranges.
items.hint: The prompt asks which position is better supported. A strong thesis takes a side on that question and previews the reasons.
items.explain:
Step 1. The prompt asks you to judge which argument is better supported, not which side you agree with.

Step 2. The first choice names the better-supported argument and previews two reasons based on evidence quality. Correct.

Step 3. “Workers deserve to know what a job pays” gives the writer's opinion on the issue instead of evaluating the arguments, which is the most common thesis mistake. “Both writers make some good points” never takes a position. “This essay will discuss” only announces the topic.

items.prompt:
Read the draft response. Then choose the option that correctly completes each blank.

Paragraph 2, blank (A): {{0}} the employers in her pilot program received 22 percent fewer applications from people who would reject the pay, they filled jobs faster, dropping from 41 days to 33 days.

Paragraph 2, blank (B): These numbers {{1}} her claim that pay ranges make hiring both faster and fairer.

options: Because
Although
However,
Instead,
support
supports
supporting
has supported

items.hint: For (A), ask how the two parts of the sentence are related: does the first part cause the second or contrast with it? For (B), find the subject and decide whether it is singular or plural.
items.explain:
Blank (A). Step 1: The sentence has two parts: fewer applications from people who would reject the pay, and jobs filled faster. Step 2: The first part explains why the second happened, so a cause word is needed. Step 3: “Because the employers … received 22 percent fewer applications …, they filled jobs faster” makes a complete sentence. Correct. “Although” signals a contrast that is not there. “However,” and “Instead,” would turn the sentence into two independent clauses joined only by a comma (a comma splice), and neither shows cause.

Blank (B). Step 1: The subject is “These numbers,” which is plural. Step 2: The draft is written in the present tense. Step 3: A plural present-tense verb is needed: “These numbers support.” Correct. “Supports” is singular. “Supporting” cannot be the main verb and leaves a fragment. “Has supported” is singular.

items.prompt: Which sentence in the draft response should be deleted because it states the writer's personal opinion on the issue instead of evaluating the two arguments?
options: “Personally, I think every job ad should list the pay, because I hate wasting time on applications.”
“Okafor's evidence comes from a real test, not a guess.”
“Okafor also cites a county review showing that the pay gap between men and women hired into the same jobs was about half as large at employers that posted ranges.”
“He describes hiring a press operator who had more experience than he expected, but one story about one hire cannot show what will happen across a whole city.”
items.hint: The task is to judge which argument is better supported. Which sentence is about the writer's own feelings instead of the writers' evidence?
items.explain:
Step 1. A GED response evaluates the arguments. It does not argue the issue from the writer's own experience.

Step 2. “Personally, I think every job ad should list the pay, because I hate wasting time on applications” is about the writer's own preference. It adds nothing to the case that Okafor's evidence is stronger. Correct: delete it.

Step 3. The other three sentences all do the job: one introduces the paragraph's point about Okafor's evidence, one cites specific evidence from Passage A, and one explains why Whitlock's anecdote is weak.

items.prompt: Each sentence below comes from a response about Passages A and B. Drag each sentence to the part of the response where it belongs.
choices: Whether employers should have to list pay in job ads is a question the Harlow City Council must now decide, and the two writers take opposite sides.
For example, Okafor reports that the average time to fill a job dropped from 41 days to 33 days during the pilot.
Whitlock, on the other hand, supports his claim with a single story about hiring one press operator.
This evidence matters because it comes from a real program with 40 employers, not from a guess.
In the end, measured results outweigh one owner's predictions, so Okafor makes the stronger case.
items.hint: Introductions set up the issue. Body paragraphs give and explain specific evidence. Conclusions wrap up the judgment.
items.explain:
Introduction: The sentence about the question the Council must decide frames the issue and names both sides. It gives no evidence, so it belongs at the start.

Body paragraph: “For example, Okafor reports …” gives specific evidence. “Whitlock, on the other hand, supports his claim with a single story” evaluates the other writer's evidence. “This evidence matters because …” explains evidence. Evidence and explanation are the work of body paragraphs.

Conclusion: “In the end, measured results outweigh one owner's predictions …” sums up the judgment. The signal phrase “In the end” and the summary of both sides mark it as a conclusion.

items.prompt:
Choose the option that correctly completes each blank in these excerpts from the draft response.

Paragraph 3, blank (C): He also predicts that the ordinance will lead the city to control {{0}} no evidence for this prediction.

Paragraph 3, blank (D): To be fair, Whitlock makes one strong point: the employers in the pilot volunteered, so {{1}} results may not apply to every business.

Paragraph 4, blank (E): The {{2}} should look closely at the evidence each writer provides.

options: wages, but he offers
wages, he offers
wages he offers
wages. But, he offering
their
there
they're
it's
Harlow City Council
Harlow city council
harlow City Council
Harlow City council

items.hint: (C) joins two complete thoughts. (D) needs a word that shows ownership. (E) is the official name of a specific government body.
items.explain:
Blank (C). Step 1: “He also predicts that the ordinance will lead the city to control wages” and “he offers no evidence for this prediction” are both independent clauses. Step 2: Two independent clauses need a comma plus a coordinating conjunction (or a period or semicolon). Step 3: “wages, but he offers” is correct. “wages, he offers” is a comma splice. “wages he offers” is a run-on. “wages. But, he offering” leaves a fragment because “offering” cannot be the main verb.

Blank (D). The results belong to the employers, so the possessive their is correct. “There” refers to a place, “they're” means “they are,” and “it's” means “it is.”

Blank (E). “Harlow City Council” is the official name of a specific body, so every word is capitalized: Harlow City Council. The other choices leave one or more words of the proper name lowercase.

items.prompt: The writer wants to replace the last sentence of the draft, “That is my opinion about the two articles,” with a stronger concluding sentence. Which choice best does this?
options: Because Okafor supports her position with tested results and answers the strongest objection, while Whitlock relies on one story and unsupported predictions, Okafor's argument is clearly the better supported of the two.
Whitlock also says that employers create the jobs the city depends on, which is another reason the Council should listen to him.
Pay range laws are becoming more common, and someday every job ad in the country may list a salary.
In the end, readers should study both articles and decide for themselves which writer is right.
items.hint: A strong concluding sentence restates the judgment and the reasons. It does not add new points or back away from the thesis.
items.explain:
Step 1. A conclusion should restate the thesis in fresh words and remind the reader of the main reasons. It should not introduce new evidence or change positions.

Step 2. The first choice restates the judgment (Okafor is better supported) and sums up both main reasons. Correct.

Step 3. The sentence praising Whitlock's “create the jobs” line adds a new point that contradicts the thesis. The sentence about future laws brings in outside speculation that neither passage supports. “Readers should … decide for themselves” abandons the writer's own judgment, which weakens the whole response.

items.prompt: Which statement best evaluates Whitlock's criticism of the pilot program in paragraph 4 of Passage B?
options: It raises a reasonable question about whether the results apply to all employers, but it overstates the point and offers no evidence that required posting would produce different results.
It proves that the pilot results were false, so Okafor's main evidence can no longer be trusted.
It is a personal attack on Okafor rather than a response to the evidence she presents.
It relies on statistics from Whitlock's own business that contradict the pilot's findings.
items.hint: Ask two questions: Is the point about volunteers reasonable? Does Whitlock give any evidence that forced posting would turn out differently?
items.explain:
Step 1. Identify the criticism. Whitlock says the 40 employers volunteered, so they were already comfortable posting pay, and their results may not predict what happens when every business must post.

Step 2. Judge it. That is a fair question about a volunteer group. But Whitlock goes further, saying the pilot “tells us nothing,” and he offers no numbers or examples showing that required posting would lead to different results. So the criticism is reasonable but overstated and unsupported. Correct.

Step 3. Eliminate the rest. The criticism does not prove the results false; it questions how widely they apply. It addresses the evidence, not Okafor as a person, so it is not a personal attack. Whitlock gives no statistics at all, from his business or anywhere else.
